---
title: "Soul's Architecture"
author: "DK"
date: "2026-05-31"
categories: [modelling]
---

One of the few advantages of aging is that you begin to see humanity not as a sea of strangers, but as a collection of familiar groups.

Even when you encounter someone for the very first time, they often seem like someone you have met before.

It is not necessarily that they look identical to an old acquaintance, but rather that they display the same underlying qualities.

This isn't a matter of us artificially forcing people into boxes based on arbitrary criteria; rather, it is that people themselves choose, through their actions and character, to be part of a certain group.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Recently, a nephew in his thirties shared a similar observation with me:

> *"I see people differently now than I did in my twenties."*

When we are young, our eyes are easily drawn to transient, exterior features. But with time, our focus shifts toward internal virtues.

Moreover, we begin to realize that these internal virtues actively shape our physical being. By the time we reach our forties, our exterior features begin to reflect that inner core.

The life we have lived, the kindness we have practiced, and the bitterness we have rejected all etch themselves into our faces.

That is precisely why my parents, in their eighties, possessed such a startling clarity of vision.

They were able to spot, analyze, and make an accurate declaration about a person within just a few seconds of a first meeting.

They were analyzing beneath the surface; they were reading the lifetime of choices written upon the stranger's face.

![](images/20260528_145538.jpg)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

A lifetime of interaction with others builds a vast, deeply personal database.

It consists of lessons painfully learned, memories deliberately discarded, and virtues we actively choose to emulate.

In our twenties, we are merely collecting raw data—experimenting, testing boundaries, and running the initial code.

As the years pass and our sample size grows, the thousands of seemingly disparate records in this internal database begin to coalesce. They train a highly refined, deeply intuitive "Large Language Model" built for our personal use.

This internal model serves a dual purpose: it acts as both an orientation guide and an immediate filter when meeting a person for the very first time.

By reading a stranger's subtle demeanor, their posture, and the cadence of their speech, we can predict the core of their character with remarkable accuracy.

This predictive accuracy scales seamlessly as we age. What began as a series of trial-and-error experiments in our youth grows into a robust, indispensable tool during middle age, ultimately becoming an exquisitely refined compass by our seventies and eighties.

![](images/cba089e7-6f84-407c-860a-5080de7c9974 (1).jpeg)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

I will continue to build, test, and train this internal model, refining its ability to read the character lines etched onto the faces of those I meet.

Yet, even as I rely on its predictive utility, I must also turn its lens inward and work relentlessly on my own qualities.

My ultimate goal is not to become a flawless predictor of humanity, but to become an outlier within the system.

I want my own life to be the data point—whether a striking anomaly or a profound confirming record—that proves people are always seeking to be whole, regardless of their current circumstances or the heavy history carved into their expressions.

I want to prove that every once in a while, even the most finely tuned model will fail in its prediction.

It *should* fail.

Because at our core, each person is uniquely endowed with a quiet, sacred capacity to persevere, defy expectations, and overcome any and all predictive models the world tries to build around them.
